Gāyatrī-mantra
(‘the मन्त्र which protects [one who] chants it’)
------------------------------------------
If there is one Vedic मन्त्र which is very much prevalent and alive even now in certain sections of the modern Hindus, it is the Gāyatrīmantra. Apart from the Ṛgveda Saṁhitā (3.62.10), it occurs in the other वेदस् also: Taittirīya Saṁhitā (1.5.6.4;

.1); Taittirīya Āraṇyaka (1.11.2); Vājasaneyī Saṁhitā (3.35; 22.9; 30.2 and 36.3); Sāmaveda Saṁhitā (1462).
This मन्त्र is said to have been revealed to the well-known sage Viśvā-मित्र. It is widely used as a part—the most important part—of the सन्ध्या ritual performed by every ब्राह्मण, twice or thrice a day.
Actually, the मन्त्र is called ‘Sāvitrī-मन्त्र’ since it is a prayer addressed to the Supreme God Savitṛ or Savitā (the Creator). However, being the very first मन्त्र revealed in the now famous गायत्री metre (a poetical mode, comprising three lines of eight letters each), the मन्त्र itself came to be known popularly as the ‘Gāyatrī मन्त्र’.
The word ‘Gāyatrī’ is sometimes defined as that (mantra) which protects (tra = to protect) one who sings or chants (gai or gāy = to sing) it.
The मन्त्र has three parts:
the व्याहृतिस्;
the Gāyatrīmantra proper;
the gāyatrīśiras.
Of course, the प्रणव or Oṁ is always added—as in the case of most of the Vedic mantras—in the beginning and is not counted.
The व्याहृतिस् are: bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ and suvaḥ.
‘Vyāhṛti’ means ‘uttering’. ब्रह्मा the creator, is said to have uttered these at the beginning of च्रेअतिओन्. Hence this appellation, ‘vyāhṛtis’.
They mean and represent the three worlds: earth, intervening space and हेअवेन्.
Sometimes, the number of these व्याहृतिस् is increased from 3 to 7, indicating the seven worlds spread over from the earth up to the सत्यलोक or ब्रह्मलोक. However, these व्याहृतिस् are used more for counting purposes in प्राणायाम than for जप.
The second part, the सावित्री-मन्त्र proper, is:
tatsavitur vareṇyaṁ
bhargo devasya dhīmahi
dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt ॥
A free translation of this मन्त्र is as follows: ‘We meditate upon that effulgence of God, the creator. May he guide our intellects!’
The third part, the gāyatrīśiras, runs thus: Om āpo jyotī raso’mṛtaṁ brahma bhūrbhuvas suvarom. It means: ‘Om. He is water, light, flavour, ambrosia and also the three worlds’.
(In effect, it means that water, light and other things are all manifestations of the ब्रह्मन् indicated by the प्रणव.)
This gāyatrīśiras too is used only in the process of prānāyāma and not in the जप of the Gāyatrīmantra.
The Gāyatrīmantra can also be used for puraścaraṇa—a particular ceremonial mode of repeating the mantra—in order to secure certain special fruits or results. The following are the usual steps involved in it: daily rituals like सन्ध्यावन्दन, worship of the goddess गायत्री, जप of the गायत्री-मन्त्र, होम (fire ritual), तर्पण (offering of water ceremonially) and feeding of the ब्राह्मणस्. However, it should be done under the guidance of experts.
In imitation of this Gāyatrīmantra, several more mantras have appeared in later literature on the various cult deities like राम, कृष्ण, शिव, देवी, गणपति and others.
See Mahānārāyaṇopaniṣad 1.22 to 33.
See also GĀYATRĪ.

Gayā
------------------------------------------
Hindu epics, धर्मशास्त्रस् and पुराणस् extol तीर्थयात्रा or पिल्ग्रिमगे very highly. It helps a person spiritually by destroying his sins and adding to his religious merit.
One of the most celebrated places of पिल्ग्रिमगे for the Hindus is गया in the गया district of Bihar. It is 88 kms. (55 miles) from the capital city Patna and is situated on the western bank of the river Phalgu.
Gayā proper, the main पिल्ग्रिमगे centre of the Hindus, is called Brahma-गया. Situated 11 kms. (7 miles) away from this is बोध्-गया, the place where Siddhārtha attained bodhi and became the बुद्ध. There is a temple here, dedicated to बुद्ध, measuring 15 metres square (50 ft.) and 48 metres (160 ft.) high. There is also a bodhi tree under which बुद्ध is said to have attained enlightenment.
According to a paurāṇic legend, Gaya was an asura (demon) who was a great devotee of विष्णु. By performing severe austerities he propitiated विष्णु and secured a boon that whoever touched him would go to हेअवेन्. As a result, all people started going to हेअवेन् just by touching him and यम’s हेल्ल् became empty! At his request, विष्णु suggested to Brahma to perform a Vedic sacrifice on Gaya’s body. Gaya agreed and the sacrifice started. But his head started shaking thus disturbing the sacrifice. In order to make it steady a stone called ‘dharmaśilā’ was secured from the world of यम and placed upon Gaya’s head. Since even this did not work, all the gods and विष्णु himself with his गदा or mace, had to stand on it, thus stopping the shaking. Gaya, the devotee, requested विष्णु that all the gods should be permanently stationed on his body. विष्णु granted the same. As a result, the place where Gaya’s body lay, became an extremely holy place.
Before starting on a पिल्ग्रिमगे to गया one should circumambulate one’s own town or village and perform a śrāddha (See ŚRĀDDHA for more details.), which is a call to the पितृस् or ancestors to come to गया.
The rites to be performed after reaching गया may be summarised as follows: digging a pit in the bed of the Phalgu river (which is dry most of the time) to get water and offer तर्पण (water for satiation of the manes) and also perform a śrāddha; twelve ancestors (three generations on the paternal and maternal side) are to be satiated by these rites; offering piṇḍas (rice-balls) at the विष्णु-pāda in the विष्णु temple (built in A.

by the queen अहल्याबाई होऌकर्) and sprinkling the holy water on oneself; offering piṇḍas at the foot of the famous अक्षयवट (See AKṢAYAVAṬA.) and honouring the ब्राह्मणस्; visit to some minor tīrthas (holy places) like Rāmaśilā and Pretaśilā hillocks.
The footprints of Lord विष्णु (Viṣṇu-pāda) in the विष्णु temple are in an octagonal basin 1.2 metres (4 ft.) in diameter and measure 40 cms. (16 inches) by 15 cms. (6 inches).
The śrāddha performed at गया is said to yield inexhaustible results. Hence once it is performed there, there is no need to do it again during the rest of one’s life.
The bodhi tree is not the original tree. However, replanting from taking the branches of the original or growing it from its seeds must have been going on for centuries. The present one was probably planted around A.

.
Many edicts of kings, mostly from South India, have been discovered at गया.

gāyatrī
------------------------------------------
The गायत्री is a celebrated Vedic छन्दस् or meter. The other well-known meters are uṣṇik, anuṣṭubh, बृहती, paṅkti, triṣṭubh and जगती.
The main reason for the गायत्री meter to be so celebrated is the revelation to the sage विश्वामित्र, of the famous सावित्री-मन्त्र in the गायत्री meter. This being the first मन्त्र in that meter and an extremely important one at that, the मन्त्र itself came to be known as the गायत्री-मन्त्र.
Consequently, the word ‘Gāyatrī’ is used not only to indicate the meter, but also the मन्त्र. In course of time it was also used to denote the presiding deity or the goddess of that मन्त्र.
There is an interesting story in the Vedic literature to prove the greatness of this meter (vide Ṛgveda 4.26.4 to 7; Taittirīya Saṁhitā

.1 to 3; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 13.25 to 28). The gist of the story is that the meter गायत्री, at the request of the देवस् or gods, took the form of a bird (Suparṇa), flew to the world of सोम and brought it (the सोम juice or अमृत, the ambrosia) to the world of gods. This story is very similar to the story of गरुड bringing अमृत from svargaloka to get his मोथेर् विनता freed from स्लवेर्य्.
Symbolically, this story may indicate that the Gāyatrīmantra which is a prayer addressed to the Supreme God in and through the orb of the sun, is capable of giving us अमृतत्व or इम्मोर्तलित्य् or लिबेरतिओन्.
The word ‘gāyatrī’ seems to have undergone gradual transmutation from meaning a Vedic meter first, the मन्त्र (addressed to Savitṛ or the creator) next and ultimately, the Vedamātā or the goddess who is the मोथेर् of the वेदस्.
This goddess has three aspects:
Gāyatrī, the feminine counterpart of ब्रह्मा and associated with the morning sun;
Sāvitrī, the feminine counterpart of विष्णु and associated with the mid-day sun;
Sarasvatī, the feminine counterpart of रुद्र, associated with the evening sun.
Iconographically, they are shown as follows:
Gāyatrī representing the Ṛgveda and ब्रह्मा, is a kumārī (young girl), red in complexion. She has two arms carrying an akṣasūtra (rosary) and a कमण्डलु (water pot). She is riding a swan.
Sāvitrī representing the Yajurveda and विष्णु is a dark complexioned yuvati (young woman). She has four arms carrying शङ्ख (conch), चक्र (discus), गदा (mace) and पद्म (lotus). She is riding on the गरुड (Viṣṇu’s eagle-mount).
Sarasvatī representing the Sāmaveda and रुद्र is a fair-complexioned vṛddhā (old woman) with four arms in which she is holding त्रिशूल (trident), डमरु (small kettle-drum), पाश (noose) and pātra (bowl). She has the Vṛṣabha or the bull as her mount.
The dhyānaśloka normally chanted at the time of the सन्ध्या ritual, however, describes गायत्री, the goddess, in a different way. She has five faces and ten arms. The five faces have the colours of muktā (pearl), vidruma (coral), hema (gold), nīla (blue) and dhavala (white). Each face has three eyes, ten arms carrying aravindayugala (two lotuses), चक्र (discus), शङ्ख (conch), गुण (trident), कपाल (skull-cup), aṅkuśa (goad), kaśa (rope or whip), abhaya and varada mudrās (handposes assuring protection and offering boons). She is seated on a lotus-seat.
This occurs in the Devībhāgavata (12.3).
